Reuters reports that seven of the children were his own. The details are horrific, and there is no value in overstating them for effect. The real point this morning is that one of the country's deadliest acts of violence this year appears to have emerged from the kind of family crisis that often sits partly hidden until the damage is irreversible.

This is a criminal investigation, but it is also a broader public-safety story. Domestic violence, mental-health strain, firearm access, prior warning signs, and failures to intervene all tend to converge after tragedies like this. The political argument will come soon enough. Before that, the practical question is whether authorities can reconstruct a timeline that shows where intervention might have been possible and why it failed.

Now to home lending, where the story remains relief with an asterisk. Freddie Mac's weekly survey, released April 16th, showed the average 30-year fixed mortgage at 6.30 percent and the 15-year fixed at 5.65 percent. That was an improvement from the week before. But daily pricing still reflects market nerves. Bankrate's Tuesday update put the current average 30-year fixed mortgage rate around 6.33 percent.

That means the direction is still better than it was a year ago, but the buyer-friendly interpretation should stay disciplined. Mortgage rates are not driven by one housing headline or one Federal Reserve sound bite. They move with the 10-year Treasury, inflation expectations, lender margins, mortgage-backed securities demand, and general market stress. If oil stays elevated because the Iran story does not settle, the same inflation fear that lifts fuel costs can also keep borrowing costs sticky.

This is the same continuity line from yesterday, but with fresher numbers behind it. You can see the improvement in the weekly survey, and you can also see how fragile that improvement is. Saxo's market note this morning put the 10-year Treasury yield at about 4.249 percent, basically unchanged from Monday's stressed levels rather than meaningfully lower. So the bond market is not yet declaring the danger passed.

For buyers, the advice does not change. Shop the full loan estimate, not the headline rate. Look at APR, points, credits, lock period, and cash to close. Test the payment at a quarter point higher than today's quote and decide whether the house still works. If it only works in the best-case scenario, it does not really work.

For sellers in Central Ohio, this remains a payment market. People can still love the location and floor plan and then walk because the monthly number is hard to defend. Strategic price cuts, repairs, and closing-cost help are still more persuasive than optimistic listing language.

Locally, the most immediate courtroom story is the retrial in the Casey Goodson Jr. case. Axios Columbus reports that jury selection is underway again for former Franklin County deputy Jason Meade in the 2020 shooting death of Goodson, after the first trial ended in a hung jury. This is one of the most consequential criminal cases in Columbus in years, not only because of the killing itself but because the retrial will again test how Franklin County handles police-use-of-force cases that divide public opinion so sharply.

The legal question is narrow even if the civic meaning is broad. Prosecutors have to prove the shooting was not justified. The defense is expected to argue self-defense. But the public importance runs wider than that. For many Columbus residents, the retrial is also a measure of whether the local justice system can produce a clear outcome in one of the city's defining accountability cases of the decade. Expect this story to move steadily through the week as jury selection continues and trial rhythm becomes clearer.

The other City Hall story with an actual countdown attached is the auditor vacancy. Columbus City Council has opened the process for replacing Megan Kilgore ahead of her May 4th resignation. The city's vacancy page makes clear that the appointee would serve until January 1, 2028, and that the office is not ceremonial. It is the city's chief accounting office, with more than 100 employees and a roughly 20 million dollar operating budget.

This is one of those stories that sounds procedural until you think about what the office actually touches. Payroll, debt, investments, tax systems, audits, and the official record of city finances all run through the auditor's operation. That is why the next few days matter. Columbus does not just need a politically acceptable name. It needs someone who can run a large financial institution inside city government on day one.

So the watch items here are applicants, qualifications, public materials, and whether Council keeps the process visible enough that residents can judge the seriousness of the appointment. Fast is acceptable. Opaque is not.

Another local civic story that remains active is the May 5th charter amendment on alternative emergency response. Axios Columbus reports the proposal would create a 24-7 program to offer non-police responses for some calls involving mental or behavioral health crises. The case for it is easy to understand. Not every emergency call is best handled by a traditional police-only response, and Columbus has spent years moving toward a broader model.

But this measure is worth following closely because implementation matters more than rhetoric. Dispatch rules, responder training, backup standards, overnight staffing, and the handoff between clinicians and police all determine whether a system like this builds confidence or confusion. With early voting underway and Election Day two weeks away, this is now close enough to count as an active story, especially if new endorsements or criticisms emerge over the next several days.

One more Columbus thread to keep in view is the women's soccer bid and McCoy Park fight. Axios reported Monday that neighborhood opposition remained strong ahead of City Council's scheduled vote on the package tied to Columbus' NWSL expansion effort. Because the public dispute is centered on McCoy Park, public access, and the public-money structure around the deal, this has become more than a sports story. It is now a process and land-use story.

I am being careful here because the actionable question for this morning is not spin but clarity. The issue to watch this week is whether Council's handling of the proposal resolves neighborhood concerns, leaves the matter unsettled, or creates a second round of backlash over transparency and park protections. Either way, the bid remains one of the city's highest-profile civic arguments.

On technology, the AI story keeps getting more physical and more expensive. Reuters, citing The Information, reported last week that OpenAI has agreed to spend more than 20 billion dollars over three years on Cerebras-powered servers, with a possible equity stake also part of the arrangement. Separate from that, Meta announced on April 14th that it is expanding its Broadcom partnership around custom AI silicon, with an initial commitment above one gigawatt and plans for a multi-gigawatt rollout over time.

That is the point Central Ohio should hear clearly: AI is not just a software race. It is a chips, power, land, cooling, networking, and financing race. Every new model feature rides on a giant industrial buildout somewhere. And Ohio remains part of that map, whether local communities welcome the attention or not.

That is why the Ohio data-center backlash still belongs in this conversation even without a brand-new headline this morning. The Ohio Newsroom has already documented how towns around the state are debating moratoriums, power demand, and local control. In practical terms, the OpenAI and Meta spending stories make that debate more urgent, not less. If the major labs and platforms are locking in that much infrastructure now, then utility costs, siting fights, and grid-capacity questions in Ohio are likely to intensify rather than fade.

Now to the market snapshot. The tone this morning is cautious but less panicked than late Sunday night. The Associated Press says world shares were mostly higher overnight even as oil remained elevated and U.S.-Iran talks stayed uncertain. TipRanks had S and P futures up about two-tenths of a percent early Tuesday, with Nasdaq futures up a bit more. Saxo put the 10-year Treasury near 4.249 percent. MarketWatch had bitcoin around 75 thousand 600 dollars late Monday, and Robinhood's early Tuesday prediction-market page implied bitcoin was hovering around 76 thousand.

The simple translation is this: investors are no longer trading as if a full energy shock is guaranteed, but they are still pricing in a world where one headline can swing oil, yields, and risk appetite in a hurry. That means today is not a day to overread one green open or one red one. The bigger relationship still matters more than the hour-by-hour moves. If oil cools and talks stabilize, stocks can breathe and rates can ease. If oil climbs again, inflation fears come back to the front of the line.

For retirement savers, the boring advice remains the correct advice. Do not rebuild a long-term plan around one geopolitical weekend. For anyone who needs cash in the next twelve months, though, this is a good reminder to check that money is actually sitting in cash or short-duration assets and not just in a portfolio you mentally marked safe.

For Columbus weather, the National Weather Service says a frost advisory remains in effect Tuesday morning, followed by a fast warm-up. After the early chill, expect mostly sunny skies and a high in the mid-70s, with gusty south winds. Tuesday night brings a chance of showers and thunderstorms, and Wednesday stays warm with more storm chances before a quieter, sunnier stretch later in the week.

The practical version is simple. It is another protect-the-plants morning, but not a coat-all-day day. Layers make sense early. By afternoon, it should feel much more like late April than the cold start suggests. Also keep an eye on the sky tonight if you are out late, because the next round of rain and thunder could arrive after dark.

The through-line this morning is that several important stories are now in their deadline phase. The U.S.-Iran ceasefire reaches its current expiration point on Wednesday, April 22nd. Mortgage relief is real, but still vulnerable to energy-driven inflation pressure. Columbus has an auditor vacancy that needs a credible replacement before May 4th. The Casey Goodson retrial is back in motion. The May 5th crisis-response vote is now close enough to move from abstract policy to active campaign. And the AI buildout story is turning national compute demand into local land and power arguments.

So watch six things today: whether Iran confirms participation in talks, whether oil holds below the worst overnight levels, whether bond yields drift lower or stay stubborn, whether the Goodson retrial produces any early procedural signals, whether auditor applicants begin to surface publicly, and whether Columbus gets any clearer answer on the NWSL and McCoy Park dispute.

That is your Morning Brief for Tuesday, April 21st. Stay alert to the midday headlines, enjoy the warmer afternoon, and assume this is another week where the calendar matters almost as much as the news itself.

item.title: Morning Brief — Morning Brief for Monday, April 20, 2026
item.description: Hormuz talks under strain, Shreveport grief, mortgage rates and oil risk, Columbus NWSL and auditor deadlines, AI infrastructure pressure, markets, and a freeze-warning Columbus forecast.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Monday, April 20th, and this is your Morning Brief.

The week starts with the same story that ended last week, but in a more dangerous form. The United States and Iran are still trying to keep a ceasefire path alive before the April 22nd deadline, while the Strait of Hormuz is again the pressure point for diplomacy, oil, and military risk.

The Associated Press reports Pakistan is still preparing for another round of U.S.-Iran talks, even after President Trump said U.S. forces seized an Iranian-flagged cargo vessel that Washington says tried to evade the blockade of Iranian ports. Iran called the seizure piracy and a ceasefire violation, and its foreign ministry said it had not yet decided whether to attend the next talks. So the headline is not simply that negotiations are scheduled. The headline is that the calendar says negotiations, while the water says confrontation.

That is the continuity from yesterday. The U.S. blockade is meant to force Tehran toward a broader settlement. Iran's restrictions on Hormuz are meant to show that pressure cuts both ways. Roughly one-fifth of the world's oil trade normally passes through the strait, along with natural gas, fertilizer inputs, and humanitarian supplies. When the strait is restricted, the risk does not stay in the Gulf. It moves into fuel prices, shipping costs, inflation expectations, Treasury yields, mortgage pricing, and household budgets.

The immediate watch item is whether Pakistan can get both sides into a room by Tuesday. A meeting with clear participation could calm markets even if the final deal is still far away. A refusal, another ship incident, or a military response from Iran would push the crisis closer to the ceasefire deadline with very little margin left. For a Columbus listener, the reason to care is practical. If oil stays elevated and inflation anxiety returns, the hoped-for relief in borrowing costs can disappear quickly.

Nationally, the other story that demands attention is grief in Shreveport, Louisiana. Authorities say a 31-year-old man killed eight children, including seven of his own, and shot two women in an attack that police describe as domestic violence. The Associated Press reports the children were between 3 and 11 years old. Police say seven children were killed inside one house and another was found on the roof after apparently trying to escape. Another child survived after jumping from the roof. The gunman died after a police pursuit.

There is no useful way to make that story neat. It is a crime story, a domestic violence story, a gun violence story, and a community trauma story all at once. It is also a reminder that some of the country's deadliest violence begins inside family conflict, where warning signs can be private, complicated, and easy for systems to miss until the danger is irreversible. The investigation now turns to the timeline, the weapons, prior contact with authorities, and whether anyone around the family saw signs that could have triggered intervention.

The political consequences will come later, and probably quickly. But this morning, the basic fact is that eight children are dead and a city is trying to understand something no city should have to absorb.

Now to home lending, where last week's improvement is meeting this morning's oil shock. Freddie Mac's April 16th survey put the average 30-year fixed mortgage at 6.30 percent, down from 6.37 percent the week before and down from 6.83 percent a year earlier. The 15-year fixed averaged 5.65 percent. Some daily rate trackers showed lower numbers by Monday morning, with NerdWallet's Zillow-based data around 6.04 percent APR for a 30-year fixed.

The honest read is that rates have improved, but they remain sensitive. A buyer may see a quote in the low sixes if the file is strong and the structure is clean. Another buyer may still be in the mid-sixes once credit, loan type, points, property type, and lock timing are included. That spread matters. So does the fact that mortgage rates are not set by one headline. They respond to Treasury yields, inflation expectations, credit spreads, lender capacity, and investor demand for mortgage-backed securities.

For buyers, this is the week to slow down and compare the full loan estimate, not just the advertised rate. Look at APR, discount points, lender credits, lock period, float-down language, cash to close, and whether the payment still works if the rate is a quarter point higher. If a slightly higher rate breaks the budget, the house is already too tight. That does not mean walk away from the market. It means do the math before the emotional part of the process takes over.

For sellers and agents, this remains a payment market. A buyer can like the kitchen, the neighborhood, and the school district, then still back away because the monthly number is hard to defend. Pricing, repairs, closing-cost credits, and rate buydown strategy can matter more than cosmetic language. In Central Ohio, where inventory is better than the frenzy years but good homes still move, the best listing strategy is the one that makes the buyer's total payment feel explainable.

Locally, Columbus City Council has a full day ahead, and the NWSL expansion package is the item with the most public heat. Council is expected to meet at 5 p.m. with a development agreement still tied to a bid for a National Women's Soccer League team. The proposal involves private investors, the city, Franklin County, public money, a proposed training facility at McCoy Park, and upgrades connected to the Crew's existing soccer infrastructure.

The Dispatch has reported that the public piece on the table includes 25 million dollars from the city and 25 million dollars from Franklin County, while private investors would put far more into launching a team if Columbus is awarded a franchise. Supporters see a chance to bring top-tier women's soccer to a city with a deep sports culture and an existing soccer identity. Opponents and skeptical residents see a rushed land decision around McCoy Park, a public-cost question, and a process that left Southwest Columbus feeling as if the site was decided before the neighborhood was fully heard.

The Southwest Area Commission has already passed a resolution opposing any proposal that gives away, trades, or reduces McCoy Park's existing footprint. That does not bind Council, but it matters politically. Area commissions exist to surface neighborhood reaction, and this reaction is direct.

The continuity point is important: this is not a simple pro-soccer versus anti-soccer fight. Columbus already has women's soccer through the Columbus Eagles and a broader local soccer ecosystem. A new NWSL team could be a major civic win. But the question before Council is whether the deal is strong enough, transparent enough, and fair enough to the neighborhood that would give up park land or accept a changed park footprint. Watch for whether Council votes, delays, amends, or adds enforceable protections around park access, replacement space, public reporting, and the proposed event-tax structure.

The other City Hall story is the auditor transition. Megan Kilgore's resignation is effective May 4th, and Council has posted the public process for appointing a replacement. The appointee would serve until January 1st, 2028, and candidates could run in 2027 to complete the term.

This office is not symbolic. The city auditor is Columbus' chief accounting officer. The office handles accounting operations, financial reporting, payroll infrastructure, debt, investments, audits, income-tax systems, and the official record of the city's finances. The 2026 salary is more than 248 thousand dollars, and the office oversees more than 100 full-time employees and a roughly 20 million dollar budget.

The best version of this appointment is fast, public, and serious. Council does not need to turn it into a campaign season, but it does need visible qualifications, applicant names, public materials, and a clear explanation of why the selected person can run a complex public-finance office on day one. The watch item over the next few days is whether credible applicants surface and whether Council keeps the process in daylight.

Also in Columbus politics, the May 5th emergency response charter amendment is moving closer. The measure would create a community crisis response system for emergency and non-emergency calls that need something other than a traditional police-only or fire-only response. Supporters frame it as a way to send clinicians, social workers, peer responders, EMTs, or other trained teams to some mental and behavioral health calls.

The idea is easy to understand. The implementation is hard. Dispatch rules have to be precise. Responders need training, backup protocols, overnight staffing, and clear authority. The city has to decide what happens when a call starts as a behavioral health crisis but becomes a safety risk in real time. Voters should listen for details, not just values. A good crisis-response system can reduce harm. A vague one can disappoint everyone involved.

On technology, the AI infrastructure story keeps getting more physical. Reuters, citing The Information, reported last week that OpenAI has agreed to spend more than 20 billion dollars over three years on servers powered by Cerebras chips, with a possible equity stake as part of the arrangement. Broadcom and Meta also extended their custom AI chip partnership through 2029, with reporting pointing to more than one gigawatt of initial compute capacity.

That is the key phrase: compute capacity. AI is often described as software, but the race is increasingly about electricity, chips, substations, cooling, water, land, and financing. Every new model feature has a supply chain behind it. Every answer from a chatbot depends on a physical system that has to be built somewhere.

That is why Ohio remains part of the story. Central Ohio and surrounding communities are already dealing with data center pressure, from New Albany to Pickaway County and beyond. The Ohio Newsroom has reported that about 18 Ohio municipalities have considered or enacted moratoriums on data centers, while residents cite noise, utility bills, wastewater, land use, and lack of transparency. Industry groups counter that data centers bring tax revenue, jobs, and investment, and say companies can cover energy costs and use better water systems.

The conflict is not going away. AI demand is rising. Local tolerance is not unlimited. The next phase will be about who pays for grid upgrades, how much information communities receive before approvals, and whether state policy favors construction so strongly that towns feel boxed in. For Columbus, this matters because data centers are no longer an abstract regional-development story. They are a power-planning story and a household-rate story.

Now the market snapshot. Reuters reported that early Monday trading turned defensive as the Hormuz story hit risk appetite. Brent crude jumped about 7 percent to roughly 96 dollars and 85 cents a barrel in early Asian trade. S&P 500 futures fell about nine-tenths of a percent. The dollar strengthened, and the yen weakened near 159 to the dollar. Saxo's morning market note had the 10-year Treasury yield around 4.27 percent after a rebound tied to oil, and Bitcoin around 74 thousand 500 dollars.

The simple version is this: markets were willing to rally last week when investors believed the worst energy scenario might be avoided. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq were near records late last week. But oil is now reminding everyone that a record market can still be nervous. If crude keeps climbing, it feeds inflation concern. If inflation concern rises, Treasury yields can climb. If yields climb, mortgage rates, stock valuations, and consumer confidence all feel it.

For retirement accounts, this is a week for discipline. If your time horizon is long, one weekend of geopolitical volatility should not rewrite the plan. If you need cash in the next year, record highs are a reminder to check that the money is actually in cash or short-term instruments, not just sitting inside a stock-heavy portfolio and labeled safe in your head.

For Columbus weather, the National Weather Service has a freeze warning in effect until 10 a.m. Monday. Around Columbus, the forecast calls for areas of frost before 10, then sunny skies with a high near 52. North wind should run around 6 to 8 miles per hour. Tonight looks mostly clear with a low around 36. Tuesday warms up quickly, with mostly sunny skies and a high near 72, then Wednesday should reach the mid-70s.

The practical version: protect early plants this morning, give the car a few extra minutes if you have frost on the glass, and dress for a chilly start even though the afternoon will be bright. This is one of those Central Ohio spring weeks where the morning feels like March and Tuesday afternoon feels like May.

The through-line this Monday is compression. The U.S.-Iran ceasefire deadline is two days away. Columbus Council could move today on a major soccer and park-land decision. The auditor vacancy has to be handled before May 4th. Voters decide the crisis-response amendment on May 5th. Mortgage rates have improved but are still exposed to oil and inflation risk. AI infrastructure is moving from earnings calls into local zoning rooms and utility planning.

So watch five things today: whether Iran commits to the Pakistan talks, whether there is any new ship incident around Hormuz, whether Columbus Council votes or delays the NWSL package, whether auditor applicants begin to emerge, and whether oil's jump shows up in Treasury yields and mortgage-rate sheets.

That is your Morning Brief for Monday, April 20th. Stay warm this morning, keep an eye on Council tonight, and treat this week like one where several deadlines are arriving at once.

The main story this morning is that the U.S.-Iran standoff has moved back into its most dangerous lane: the Strait of Hormuz. Over the last day, Iran again moved to close or restrict the strait after the United States refused to lift its blockade of Iranian ports. The Associated Press reports President Trump says U.S. delegations will head to Pakistan to resume ceasefire talks, but the diplomacy is now happening under direct pressure from shipping, oil, and military risk.

This is the continuation of the blockade story we have been tracking all week, only with less room for error. The ceasefire clock still points to April 22nd. Pakistan has been trying to keep both sides at the table. The United States is using maritime pressure to force Iran to accept a broader settlement. Iran is using Hormuz to remind Washington and the oil market that it can raise the cost of pressure quickly.

The immediate danger is not just a formal collapse of talks. It is an accident, a misread signal, or one ship inspection that turns into a confrontation. Roughly one-fifth of the world's oil moves through the Strait of Hormuz, so even a partial disruption can affect crude prices, shipping insurance, gasoline expectations, and inflation psychology. That is why this story belongs at the top of a local morning brief in Columbus. The line from the Gulf to a Central Ohio household runs through fuel, freight, groceries, interest rates, and monthly payments.

The practical watch item today is whether Pakistan can put a firm U.S.-Iran meeting on the calendar before Wednesday. If a meeting is announced with a clear agenda, oil markets may treat that as a pressure release. If there is no meeting, or if either side reports a new clash at sea, markets may reopen tonight with a much more defensive tone.

In Washington, Congress bought itself only a little more time on surveillance powers. President Trump signed a short-term extension of Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, keeping the authority alive until April 30th. Section 702 allows U.S. intelligence agencies to collect foreign communications without a warrant, but the collection can also sweep in Americans' messages when they are communicating with people overseas.

The argument is familiar, but the deadline is new. National security officials say the program is essential for tracking threats outside the United States. Civil liberties advocates say the government should need a warrant before searching Americans' communications that were incidentally collected. The short extension means Congress has not settled the bigger fight. It has simply moved the deadline into the end of the month.

The other national political story is more symbolic, but still revealing. A federal appeals court has temporarily allowed construction to continue on President Trump's planned White House ballroom while litigation moves forward. The project has drawn a legal challenge from preservation advocates who argue the administration bypassed required approvals for a major addition on the White House grounds. A hearing is now scheduled for June 5th.

The reason to keep that story in the brief is not the ballroom itself. It is the broader governing question: how much can an administration do through executive control of federal property, private donations, emergency arguments, or fast-moving construction before courts and Congress catch up? That same pattern shows up in immigration, tariffs, surveillance, and federal funding. The venue changes, but the institutional fight is the same.

Now to home lending. Mortgage rates are still better than they were a few weeks ago, but the improvement is not enough to change the basic affordability math. Freddie Mac's April 16th survey put the average 30-year fixed mortgage at 6.30 percent, down from 6.37 percent the week before and down from 6.83 percent a year earlier. NerdWallet's Zillow-based data early this morning had the 30-year fixed average around 6.05 percent APR, ten basis points lower than a week ago.

So the honest read is this: buyers are seeing low-to-mid sixes depending on loan type, credit profile, points, lender, and timing. That is a better conversation than sevens, but it is not a cheap-money market. In Central Ohio, the purchase price, taxes, insurance, maintenance, and school-district premium still decide whether the payment works.

For buyers, the weekend rule is simple. Do not compare only the rate. Compare the rate, APR, points, lender credits, lock period, float-down language, and cash to close. A quote with a lower rate can still be worse if it is bought down with fees you do not understand. If you are shopping this weekend, run the payment at today's quote and again a quarter point higher. If the second number breaks the budget, the house is not actually affordable yet.

For sellers, this is a payment market. A buyer may like the house and still hesitate because the monthly number feels stretched. That means pricing, concessions, and repairs matter more than they did during the frenzy years. A clean inspection item or a closing-cost credit may do more than a dramatic listing description. The goal is to make the buyer's payment easier to defend.

Locally, the biggest government deadline is tomorrow. Columbus City Council is expected to meet Monday at 5 p.m., and the NWSL expansion package remains the most watched item around that meeting. The deal under discussion would connect public commitments from the city and Franklin County with a private-investor bid to bring a National Women's Soccer League team to Columbus. The sticking point is McCoy Park, where a proposed training facility has triggered opposition from residents and the Southwest Area Commission.

The continuity point from Friday still applies: this is not a simple pro-soccer versus anti-soccer story. Columbus already has a women's soccer community, including the Columbus Eagles. A new top-tier franchise could be a major win for the city, but the land question, public cost, and neighborhood process are the test. When a city says a site cannot change because the bid has already been submitted, residents hear that the public part of the process arrived after the private part.

Tomorrow's question is whether Council votes, delays, amends, or tries to add enforceable protections for McCoy Park. Watch especially for any change to the two percent event-tax structure, any promise about replacement park space, and any public explanation of how the proposed NWSL team would coexist with the soccer organizations already here.

The other City Hall story is the auditor transition. Columbus now has an official vacancy process posted for replacing City Auditor Megan Kilgore, who is resigning effective May 4th for a private-sector role connected to municipal finance. The city page says Council's appointee would serve until January 1st, 2028, with candidates able to run in 2027 to complete the rest of the term. The job pays $248,345 in 2026 and oversees more than 100 full-time employees and a roughly 20 million dollar office budget.

That salary number is not trivia. It tells you the scale and seriousness of the office. The auditor is Columbus' chief accounting officer. The office manages the city's official financial record, income-tax systems, accounting operations, payroll infrastructure, debt, investments, audits, and financial reporting. In plain English, this is one of the offices that determines whether the city can budget honestly, borrow credibly, and keep the machinery running.

The best-case version of the appointment process is public, fast, and rigorous. Council does not need a months-long search, but it does need clear qualifications, visible applicant materials, and a chance for residents to understand why the appointee is ready to run a complex public-finance operation. The watch item over the next few days is whether applicants begin to surface and whether Council gives the process real daylight.

The proposed amendment would create a community crisis response system for emergency and non-emergency calls that need a different response from a traditional police-only or fire-only dispatch. Axios Columbus has described it as a possible path toward round-the-clock alternatives for some mental and behavioral health calls.

The idea is straightforward. Some calls need clinicians, social workers, peer responders, EMTs, or other trained teams who can de-escalate and connect people to care. The implementation is the hard part. Columbus would have to define dispatch rules, responder safety protocols, overnight staffing, training, data reporting, and coordination with county and state systems.

For voters, the useful question is not whether a crisis-response system sounds good in theory. It is whether the charter language creates enough obligation for the city to build it well, and enough flexibility for the people running it to adjust when real calls get complicated. Expect supporters to talk about right response, right professional, and prevention. Expect skeptical voters to ask who responds when a call changes from behavioral health to safety risk in real time.

On technology, the AI story continues to leave the software screen and land on the power grid. Meta and Broadcom have expanded a custom-chip partnership through 2029, with an initial commitment of more than one gigawatt of computing capacity. That is a huge physical footprint for something that consumers experience as an app feature or a chatbot answer. It means chips, networking gear, cooling systems, substations, water, land, and long-term power contracts.

TSMC, the world's leading contract chipmaker, also reinforced the same point last week. Its quarterly profit jumped sharply on AI demand, and the company pointed to continued strength in advanced semiconductors and packaging. The market is telling us that the AI buildout is still alive. Communities are telling us that the buildout has costs.

That is the Ohio angle. Data centers can bring investment and tax base, but they also raise questions about who pays for grid upgrades, how much water is used, how land is changed, and whether electricity customers subsidize infrastructure built for a handful of very large technology companies. Maine lawmakers just passed the country's first statewide moratorium on large data centers, according to the Washington Post, and other states are debating similar pauses. Ohio has not gone that far, but the political pressure is moving in that direction whenever residents feel the benefits and costs are not being shared clearly.

Now the market snapshot. The latest settled AP market board from late last week showed stocks still near records. On Thursday, the S&P 500 rose 0.3 percent to 7,041.28, the Dow gained 0.2 percent to 48,578.72, and the Nasdaq climbed 0.4 percent to 24,102.70. The rally has two engines. First, investors are still rewarding AI, chip, and technology names. The renewed Hormuz closure means oil, gold, Treasury yields, and stock futures matter more than usual tonight. A record market can still be a nervous market.

For retirement accounts, the Sunday read is balance. New highs are good. They also make portfolios more exposed to disappointment if diplomacy fails. If you have cash needs in the next year, do not let an index record convince you that risk disappeared. If you are investing for decades, do not let one scary weekend headline turn a long plan into a short reaction.

The National Weather Service forecast for Columbus called for mostly sunny skies with a high near 57, after Saturday's showers and a colder night. Tonight should be mostly clear with lows in the mid-30s. Monday looks sunny but still cool, with highs in the mid-50s before temperatures start climbing again Tuesday.

The practical version: today is a decent day for errands, a walk, or getting the yard reset after rain, but it will not feel like the warm stretch we had earlier in the week. Keep a jacket handy this morning and again after sunset. Gardeners should pay attention to the overnight lows tonight and Monday night, especially in colder suburbs and low-lying spots.

The through-line this morning is compression. The U.S.-Iran ceasefire deadline is three days away. Columbus Council could move on the NWSL package tomorrow. Housing data arrives this week with buyers still stuck between better rates and high payments. The auditor vacancy has to be handled before May 4th.
